    #89974. “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his fresh book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • It has been revealed that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his fresh book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he stated, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    It has been revealed that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    Industry observers note that for most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Recent findings suggest that against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    It has been revealed that the court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    Industry observers note that but I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    Recent findings suggest that another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    According to recent reports, that leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    Recent findings suggest that alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    Sources indicate that as I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    Recent findings suggest that the administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    Industry observers note that pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Recent findings suggest that specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    In a recent development, the 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    Alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the new term.

    The 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    In a recent development, so Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the problem-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    Dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    Industry observers note that recommended Citation: Taraleigh Davis, “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/im-afraid-this-is-going-to-continue-justice-alito-the-executive-and-the-emergency-docket/.

    #89962. Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1853 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • Sources indicate that in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • Recent findings suggest that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    Sources indicate that in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    Recent findings suggest that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    Sources indicate that originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    Industry observers note that for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    In a recent development, similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    According to recent reports, for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual customers of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    Recent findings suggest that this criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Finally, and most important in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    According to recent reports, sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    Recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    Bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    It has been revealed that many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    Industry observers note that from an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Industry observers note that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky says, courts must decide: which tradition?

    In a recent development, the existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at issue in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    Recommended Citation: Haley Proctor, Listening to the past, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/listening-to-the-past/.

    #89960. Breaking: 2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1039 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before.
    • Recent findings suggest that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors.
    • It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

    Recent findings suggest that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

    It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

    Recent findings suggest that trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize plans and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

    In a recent development, AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect users and the public at large.

    At Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate newly introduced AI-driven workflows into their firms.

    Recent findings suggest that drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report shows that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

    The growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a new category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

    Recent findings suggest that as AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow consumers to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

    Partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were newly introduced products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

    Litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

    As upcoming AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to rapidly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

    Sources indicate that nicole Black is a Rochester, Latest York-based attorney, author and journalist. She is the principal legal insight strategist at 8am, parent organization of LawPay, MyCase, CasePeer and DocketWise. She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association. She writes regular columns for ABAJournal.com and Above the Law, has authored hundreds of articles for other publications, and she regularly speaks at conferences regarding the intersection of law and emerging technologies. Follow her on LinkedIn, or she can be reached at [email protected].

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    #89950. Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2403 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.
    • Industry observers note that the court previously unveiled, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v.
    • Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    Industry observers note that the court previously unveiled, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services tech giant violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    The research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    It has been revealed that thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    In June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    Sources indicate that in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    Sources indicate that in their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Industry observers note that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    It has been revealed that khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    After the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they said, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    It has been revealed that the Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the issue at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    Sources indicate that in rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Fresh York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    According to recent reports, maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at issue in this case, the state remarked, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    Industry observers note that in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    Strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At problem in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Industry observers note that gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    It has been revealed that and in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    In its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Newly introduced York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    It has been revealed that the United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    It has been revealed that justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    • On Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in dozens of cases, including two DEI-related disputes – the first, a challenge from University of California scholars to cuts in research funding; the second, a challenge from California doctors to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses – and a Second Amendment clash over Maryland laws prohibiting guns in “sensitive places.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Forty-six years ago today, the Supreme Court issued its ruling in Stone v. Graham, holding that a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause because it “has no secular legislative purpose.” That 1980 ruling is back in the spotlight this term, as the court considers whether to take up challenges to similar Ten Commandments laws in Texas and Louisiana.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in dozens of cases, including two DEI-related disputes – the first, a challenge from University of California scholars to cuts in research funding; the second, a challenge from California doctors to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses – and a Second Amendment clash over Maryland laws prohibiting guns in “sensitive places.”.

    The court also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

    For more on Monday’s order list, see the Morning Reads and On Site sections below.

    Sources indicate that the December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.

    #89936. Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1906 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause.
    • 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.
    • According to recent reports, colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

    At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

    Recent findings suggest that st. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

    According to recent reports, colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”.

    In a recent development, st. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free exercise of religion as it requires them to accept students whose families do not adhere to the Catholic Church’s teachings, including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. The federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law.

    It has been revealed that the 10th Circuit stressed that the Colorado law did not discriminate on the basis of religion. The court applied the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the free exercise clause cannot be used to challenge a neutral law of general applicability. This means that the free exercise clause is not a basis for an exception to a law unless it can be shown either that it was motivated by a desire to interfere with religion, that it discriminates against religion, or even that it just creates discretion to treat religions differently from secular actions. The 10th Circuit found that the Colorado law met the requirements for a neutral law of general applicability, as, among other things, it did not treat any one religion differently than others.

    Recent findings suggest that the court of appeals also found no discrimination against religious schools in government funding. In 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, the court declared unconstitutional a Missouri law that provided public and secular private schools funds for surfacing playgrounds that did not provide the same funds to religious schools. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, the court applied this to invalidate a Maine law that provided funds to parents to send their children to secular private schools in areas without public schools, but not “sectarian” schools. The 10th Circuit distinguished these cases, explaining that the Colorado law did not exclude religious schools as it allowed them to receive state money on the same terms as all other preschools.

    At the oral argument on Nov. 3, there was more focus on the latter problem, perhaps because it would avoid the court needing to decide whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a concurring opinion, expressing support for that view, but finding it unnecessary to decide the issue to resolve that case. The court likely remains divided over whether to overrule Smith and what would replace it.

    In the arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there were many questions from the conservative justices that suggested that they saw the Colorado law as discriminatory because of its effects on religious schools. For example, Chief Justice John Roberts asked the attorney for Colorado how this was different from the program in Carson v. Makin and stated that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here,” as it disadvantaged religious schools. Barrett asked Colorado’s attorney why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can nevertheless “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows such “schools will be unable to agree to.”.

    In other words, these justices suggested that a discriminatory effect of Colorado’s law would be sufficient to find the law violated the free exercise of religion even though the law remarked nothing about religion and was not motivated by a desire to interfere with religion. The questions suggested that Colorado adopting the non-discrimination requirement knowing that some religious schools would not comply should be sufficient to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause.

    According to recent reports, such an approach would be dramatically different from analysis under the equal protection clause. Although I personally think such cases were incorrectly decided, the Supreme Court long has held that proof of a discriminatory effect alone is not sufficient to establish race or sex discrimination. And it has expressly held that discrimination cannot be proven by showing that government officials took an action with knowledge that it would have discriminatory consequences.

    Industry observers note that washington v. Davis, decided 50 years ago, was a key case holding that a racially discriminatory effect is not sufficient to establish an equal protection violation. Applicants for the police force in Washington, D.C., were required to take a test, and statistics revealed that Black individuals failed the examination much more often than Whites. The Supreme Court, however, held that proof of a discriminatory impact is insufficient, by itself, to show the existence of a racial classification. Justice Byron White, writing for the majority, mentioned that the court never had held that “a law or other official act, without regard to whether it reflects a racially discriminatory purpose, is unconstitutional solely because it has a racially disproportionate impact.” The court explained that discriminatory impact, “[s]tanding alone, . . . does not trigger the rule that racial classifications are to be subjected to the strictest scrutiny and are justifiable only by the weightiest of considerations.”.

    The court has even held that discriminatory purpose cannot be proven by showing that government officials adopted a policy with knowledge that it would have a discriminatory effect. Rather, the court has made it clear that showing such a purpose requires proof that the government desired to discriminate. In 1979’s Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts v. Feeney, the court declared: “‘Discriminatory purpose,’ … implies more than intent as volition or intent as awareness of consequences. It implies that the decisionmaker . . . selected or reaffirmed a particular course of action at least in part ‘because of,’ not merely ‘in spite of,’ its adverse effects upon an identifiable group.”.

    It has been revealed that feeney involved a challenge to a Massachusetts law that gave preference in hiring for state jobs to veterans. At the time of the litigation, more than 98% of the veterans in the state were male, and only 1.8% were female. The result was a substantial discriminatory effect against women in hiring for state jobs. Nonetheless, based on the principles articulated above, the Supreme Court held that there was not a sex classification because the law creating a preference for veterans was facially sex neutral and there was not proof that the state’s purpose in adopting the law was to disadvantage women. The fact that the legislature knew there would be an discriminatory effect against women was thus irrelevant.

    Recent findings suggest that there is no way to reconcile this equal protection jurisprudence with the approach several conservative justices suggested in St. Mary Catholic Parish. The question then becomes whether there is any reason to treat discrimination under the free exercise clause differently from under the equal protection clause.

    Industry observers note that several justices suggested in their questions at oral argument that Sherbet v. Verner, a 1963 case, justifies concluding that discriminatory impact is alone sufficient for a free exercise violation. That case involved a state having denied unemployment benefits to a woman, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, who quit her job rather than work on her Saturday Sabbath. The court concluded that the denial of benefits imposed a substantial burden on religion; the woman had to choose between an income and her faith. The court thus said that the problem was “whether some compelling state interest enforced in the eligibility provisions of the . . . statute justifies the substantial infringement of appellant’s First Amendment right.” The court found no such compelling interest and ruled that the denial of benefits constituted a violation of the free exercise clause.

    Sherbert found a violation of the free exercise of religion based on the impact on her religion despite the law at matter being facially neutral. As a precedent for striking down the Colorado law, however, that is unpersuasive. Sherbert was decided a decade before the Supreme Court held that proof of discriminatory impact was not sufficient for an equal protection violation. And although the court has not overruled Sherbert, it has never explained how it can be reconciled with Employment Division v. Smith. But most importantly, invoking Sherbert begs the crucial question: Should a different standard be used for discrimination under the free exercise clause compared to the equal protection clause?

    Conceptually, I cannot understand any reason why discrimination on the basis of religion should be treated dissimilarly from discrimination based on race or sex. Why should two such critical rights be treated differently? Indeed, it is just a doctrinal accident that religious discrimination is litigated under the free exercise clause (or the establishment clause) rather than the equal protection clause.

    According to recent reports, applying equal protection principles, the Colorado law does not discriminate against religion in its terms or in its purpose. Many commentators, including me, have argued that – despite court precedent – discriminatory impact should be enough for a claim under equal protection. But there has been no suggestion from the court that it is moving in that direction.

    Finally, it is key to stress that even if the law is deemed discriminatory, that does not mean that it is automatically unconstitutional. It means that strict scrutiny should be applied, in which the government action can be upheld if there is a compelling purpose for it. I was disappointed that the conservative justices did not focus on the government’s compelling interest in preventing children from being discriminated against on account of their gender identity or for having LGBTQ parents. Without explicitly saying so, the justices appear poised to carve out a special place for the free exercise clause over that of equal protection.

    Recent findings suggest that erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

    Recent findings suggest that recommended Citation: Erwin Chemerinsky, Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 17, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/treating-the-free-exercise-of-religion-and-equal-protection-differently/.

    • This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Data API Engineer to join our Data API Team and help improve the feature set, reliability and performance of our Data API, based on the PostgREST project.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Work on PostgREST’s PostgreSQL driver (based on Hasql) and remove bottlenecks and improve it’s performance.

    Work on PostgREST development of new features and bug fixes, aligned towards the goal of a multitenant Data API.

    Resolve incidents and escalated support challenges, while also improving observability and performance.

    Collaborate cross-functionally with other teams to debug and solve integration issues with the Supabase platform.

    Strong Haskell skills with at least 3 years of experience.

    Experience using the C language.

    Solid knowledge of SQL and plpgsql scripting in PostgreSQL.

    Strong track record of contributing to and engaging with open-source projects. Bonus points if you’ve maintained an open source project.

    Strong experience with providing technical support to users with varying levels of technical expertise.

    Experience with debugging applications under the Linux operating system.

    Sources indicate that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    • A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.
    • The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A recent Latest York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani looks to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Industry observers note that additionally, the newly introduced law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani said.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    #89929. Tech Report: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1586 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that on Oct.
    • According to recent reports, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that on Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    According to recent reports, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    Industry observers note that section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    Recent findings suggest that for the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    As for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, stated fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    The Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    Recent findings suggest that but a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Recent findings suggest that judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    Sources indicate that the 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, Fresh Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    Sources indicate that if the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    Industry observers note that that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process problem. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    According to recent reports, rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    #89925. Industry News: Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (975 w)

    Industry News: Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog
